pages.burden-release-guide.body.p001.tex.text: Weight and pressure has gravity. Do you recognize feelings that arise — frustration, guilt, shame, or just something that shows up when certain conditions are met — that you never seem to be able to let go of, because you didn't know how?
Not a requirement. Not a performance. Just a menu.

pages.burden-release-guide.body.div002.p.text: Most people don't notice they're carrying weight because they've been carrying it long enough that it feels like just — them. It isn't. Find the one that fits what arrived today. Return that. Close the page. Go back to living.

pages.burden-release-guide.body.div003.d.text: Before You Begin
How this actually works
Speaking or writing is the mechanism. A thought that stays a thought doesn't move the same way...
Speaking or writing is how this works.
A thought that stays a thought doesn't move the same way. The intention needs a vehicle — your voice, your handwriting, a typed sentence. Something that leaves the inside of you.
It doesn't have to be long. It doesn't have to be polished. Even a whisper counts. Even one sentence written down. The act of externalizing it is what signals the release.
One thing at a time. Don't work through the whole list. Find the one that fits right now and return that one. If nothing fits, use #15:
"Holy Father God, I don't know what this is. Here. Hold this."
What to Expect
How the body responds
The body responds differently for each person. The absence of a dramatic response doesn't mean nothing moved...
The body responds differently for each person. The absence of a dramatic response doesn't mean nothing moved — sometimes the quietest signals are the deepest ones.
A rise in the throat
— pressure before release, followed by a spontaneous exhale or cool release of air. The nervous system completing something it had been holding.
A breath that arrives on its own
— a deep inhale, yawn, or sigh you didn't decide to take.
Eyes watering
— not necessarily crying. Moisture arriving, especially when something has been held a long time without being seen.
Muscle release
— shoulders dropping, jaw unclenching. Often you don't notice how much tension was there until it leaves.
Tingling
— hands, arms, chest, or face. Something moving through areas that were previously held.
A sudden dry heave
— startling but brief. The body attempting to expel something that isn't physical. Common when something long suppressed gets permission to move. It passes quickly.
Quiet absence
— sometimes nothing obvious. Just a sense that something is slightly less present than it was. Like a hum that stopped.
This section is a living document. More responses will be added as they are gathered. Your experience may look different from all of these — that doesn't disqualify it.
If You Don't Trust God Yet
The name doesn't have to be God to start
What matters is what you are actually returning the weight to. A concept won't hold it...
The name doesn't have to be God to start. What matters is what you are actually returning the weight to.

A concept won't hold it — "the universe," "my higher self," "positive energy" as an idea rather than a felt presence will bounce the burden back, often as confusion or shame. A felt presence, whatever you call it, can hold it.
If you're unsure, test it. Return the same burden to three different names and notice which one actually dissolves the weight versus which one just moves it.
Your body will tell you. Not your mind.

Not because God is a better container. Because God is not a container at all. Weight returned to God does not bounce back — it ceases to be weight. The name points to the asymptote: the place where weight goes to stop being weight.
If the practice keeps returning weight rather than dissolving it, the container may not be deep enough. The door to God stays open — not as a requirement, as an option when you're ready to try it.
